summary:
## Overview
This guide details the complete process for creating durable, professional-looking embroidered iron-on patches, ideal for quickly making uniforms for volunteers and organizations.

## Materials & Costs
- **Embroidery Supplies**: Two sheets of **thick cutaway stabilizer**.
- **Finishing Supplies**: **UltraHold HeatnBond** fusible sheet, small **curved scissors**, and a **lighter**.
- **Application**: A hot iron and a garment (e.g., t-shirt or polo).
- **Costs**: The video breaks down the material cost per patch and discusses pricing for selling finished patches versus donating them.

## Patch Finishing Workflow
After the design is embroidered, follow these steps for a clean finish.

1.  **Trimming**: Use large scissors for a rough cut, then use **curved scissors** to trim as close to the satin stitch border as possible without cutting the threads.
2.  **Sealing Edges**: Quickly and carefully pass the flame from a **lighter** around the cut edge of the patch. This melts the white stabilizer, causing it to retract and hide behind the border threads.
    > [!IMPORTANT]
    > Do not hold the flame in one spot for too long. Keep it moving to avoid scorching the patch threads.
3.  **Applying Fusible Backing**:
    *   Place the **HeatnBond** sheet on the back of the patch with the textured (adhesive) side down.
    *   Using a hot iron on its highest setting, press down on the patch in 6-second intervals.
    *   Continue pressing until the adhesive melts and the backing paper looks translucent or "wet," indicating the glue has bonded.
    *   Let the patch cool completely so the adhesive can harden.
4.  **Final Trim & Peel**:
    *   Trim any excess HeatnBond paper from around the patch.
    *   Carefully peel the paper backing off to reveal the shiny, solid layer of adhesive.

## Application to Garment
- **Placement**: A simple technique for left-chest placement is to align the patch with the midpoint of the sleeve opening and the edge of the collar.
- **Ironing**:
    *   Press the patch firmly with a hot iron in 6-second intervals until it is fully bonded to the fabric.
    > [!TIP]
    > Place a piece of scrap fabric or a pressing cloth over the patch before ironing. This protects the embroidery threads from direct heat, preventing melting or damage.

## Introduction to Iron-On Patches

Hey guys, it's Willie here again with another episode of Embroidery Hub. We'll be making iron-on transfer patches for volunteers. These patches can be ironed on to a t-shirt or polo to make quick uniforms for those organizations in need of volunteers.

Now if you want this embroidery design to make patches of your own, then stay to the end of the video and we will let you know where to get them. Now remember to Like and Subscribe for more tutorials. Let's get started.

## Materials, Costs, and Profit Potential

Alright, so these are the materials we're going to be using today. We have our scissors like always. This time we will use the small scissors with a little curve to it to cut around the edge and make a nice clean cut. We have our lighter for burning the stabilizer around the edge of the patch to hide it inside of the threads. And we're going to be using two sheets of thick cutaway stabilizer.

Here we have the UltraHold HeatnBond fusible sheet and our hoop with a shirt to attach the patch. So to make this patch we spent 25 cents for each stabilizer, a total of 50 cents for both since we're using two. Now out of this we can actually make four patches but today for video purposes we're only making one.

Now this is the UltraHold HeatnBond. This cost us $2.14 in a Jo-Ann store for one yard. Out of this one yard you can make over a hundred of these. So we looked up on Etsy how much you can sell these patches for. They range around three to seven dollars, but of course you can donate them to help out the community.

Now if you guys want to sell the patch included with the shirt, this shirt we bought for four dollars. If you buy in a bigger batch you're probably gonna get it for around two to three dollars. You can make a little extra on it.

## Hooping the Stabilizer and Machine Setup

Alright guys, so for a first step, we're going to hoop it. I'm going to be putting first bottom part and the top. Make sure you squeeze it nice and tight like a drum. And now we're going to go to the machine and put it in the machine.

Alright guys, so today we have the Ricoma MT 1501 machine. The cool thing about this machine is that it comes with a sash frame, so you're able to do a dozen at a time. But for the purpose of the video today, we're just gonna be doing one.

## Setting Up and Embroidering the Patch

Alright, let's get started. Alright, so we're gonna go into our panel and we're gonna change over to our patch file. I'm already unlocked. Let me go ahead and choose my patch file. It's going to be the last one here. I'm gonna press okay. Now remember you should be able to do this with any machine—one needle embroidery machines all the way up to the 15 needle machines.

Let's go and lock it. And we already have our color sequence already located here. You don't need to put any pause on this since there's a patch; it's going to go right through it. Should take about less than 10-15 minutes to make. Yeah, that's about it. Let's go ahead and trace and press the start button. You can do this on any machine, even on a single needle. And remember that we will be letting you know where to get this free embroidery design at the end of the video.

## Unhooping and Trimming the Embroidered Patch

All right, so now we're all done. The next step is going to be unhooping it and cutting around the edge. So I'm going to use just the big scissors there just to go quick cut. Now I'm going to use these curved scissors so I can go right on the edge. I'm going to be turning it around. Using the same scissors I'm going to snip out any excess thread. Also, if you're interested in learning how to make other in-demand items like this one, check out other videos you can find under the description below or by clicking on the cards above.

## Sealing the Edges with Heat

Alright, so now I'm gonna use this lighter. You can use any lighter, works fine with it. And you're going to be burning the edge. I'm just gonna go like this and just keep turning it. Don't leave it there for too long. Alright, you can tell how the white's already starting to disappear. You could even go and just go just on top of it and any little threads that might be there, they're all gonna shrink and get really nice and tight. You could do the same thing to the back. That's it.

## Applying the HeatnBond Fusible Backing

So because we are using a plastic table, I'm going to put a shirt over it just so it doesn't melt down and don't lose any registration on this. So the next step is very simple. I'm just gonna flip it around and get your HeatnBond. Make sure you have the texture side on the back. So what I'm going to do is just make my life a little easier by cutting just a little bit closer and put it right on the shirt. We're gonna use our iron now and place it down for six seconds at a time. You want to make sure that the glue gets stuck to the patch. So once you're doing this, after six seconds, just view it. You can start seeing on this area now it looks like it's kind of wet, which is actually the glue that's becoming like a liquid form. And then after this we're just gonna stop and let it sit for a half so it gets cold and it gets hardened again.

I have this iron set to 6, which is the hottest it gets, and I'm applying some pressure on this patch. So I'm sure I'm getting all the sides all around the patch as much as I can possible. If you need to do this process again, you can do it. It's not gonna make any difference to the actual patch. So you can actually use multiple sheets of the sticky material if you need to, and just keep doing this process until you see the paper become seeped like in these spots. I'm gonna show you in a minute now how it looks exactly. So what you want is to be able to see through the paper as you can see here. Alright, and now we're just gonna place it down and let it rest for a couple of minutes.

## Final Trim and Peeling the Backing Paper

Alright, so now we're going to be cutting the edge with your curved scissors. Let's get it as close as we possibly can. Alright, and there you go. Now let's just take the back piece off. And you can see the shiny part, this is the glue stuck to it.

## Ironing the Patch onto the Garment

Alright, so that's how it should look. Let's go ahead and iron it on to a shirt now. Alright, so now we're gonna place the patch on the left chest. And the way I did that is by getting half of your sleeve, and right on this edge of the neck will be right in the middle of it. I'm going to use another fabric to just place it on top so I don't damage my patch. And just do the same process. You're going to leave it for six seconds. You can move it around, and every six seconds just let it go and take a look at it. All right, so I'm gonna let it go, take a look at it. Okay, it's looking good. If you'd like to see how we digitized this patch, just let us know in the comments below, and we will make sure to make future videos showing you the process.

## Conclusion and Resources

Alright, we're all set. Alright, that's it guys. This is how you make an iron-on patch from start to finish. We really would like to thank all the volunteers and organizations making a difference out there and we hope these patches play a part in helping all of you.

You guys can do this with any machine. We're going to be posting on the link below the PES file so you can use on any of the other machines you guys have, even a one needle machine. If you guys liked this video, make sure to hit that subscribe button and let us know if you have any questions about this project in the comments below. Also, if you want to connect with other apparel decorators like myself, join our free Facebook group Embroidery and Custom Apparel Mastery. There you can ask questions and join the community. Also for the latest in the world of decorated apparel, follow us on Instagram @RicomaHQ.

Alright guys, thanks for watching and we will see you next time.
